definitionFindings: The equality passage explicitly tests self-evident moral standing through measurable differences; the critique identifies that empirical-versus-normative switch, rather than merely an unsupported egalitarian premise.
The humanity courtroom passage moves from a class containing different people to one disqualified litigant; the frozen critique identifies precisely that collective-versus-individual ambiguity.

The impersonal-good passage calls the highest good incapable of goodness and therefore neither good nor bad; the accepted label concerns the shift from evaluative foundation to an agent's virtue, not merely a preference for personal grounding.

Folley's cross passage explicitly moves from observers not being compelled to a clearly nondeductive relationship; the critique identifies the distinction between psychological persuasion and logical entailment.

The two red-herring decisions concern substitution of intellectual history or foundational impasse for requested justificatory or scriptural assessment, not every partial answer or unfinished argument.

The Buddhist reflection reply presupposes Christ's universal illumination to classify the offered independent alternative as derivative; confirmation bias was rejected as duplicating the same mechanism without separate evidential filtering.
The evolutionary reply changes causal survival into a prescribed ethic; disturbing examples alone were not additionally labeled base-rate neglect or red herring.
The outrage reply treats felt experience as testimony against subjective morality, supporting subjective validation already identified in its critique; the separate belief-bias proposal was rejected.
Citation, historical compression, a disputed premise, incomplete universalization, and failure to exclude rivals were not automatically assigned nearby catalog labels.
